provenance.author: Capabilio
provenance.note: Original questions written for Capabilio's baseline check. Not copied from any course, book, exam or question bank.

items.prompt: total = 0. Repeat for i = 1, 2, 3, 4: if i is even, add i to total. What is total at the end?
items.explanation: Only 2 and 4 are even, and 2 + 4 = 6.

items.prompt: n = 10 and count = 0. While n > 1: set n to n divided by 2 (integer division, rounding down) and add 1 to count. What is count when the loop ends?
items.explanation: n goes 10 → 5 → 2 → 1, which takes 3 steps.

items.prompt: for i = 0 to 4: for j = i to 4: run the body once. How many times does the body run in total?
items.explanation: The inner loop runs 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 times: 15 in total.

items.prompt: A zero-indexed array is [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]. What is the element at index 3?
items.explanation: Index 0 is 4, index 1 is 8, index 2 is 15 and index 3 is 16.

items.prompt: You reverse a string of length 7 in place by swapping characters from both ends towards the middle. How many swaps are needed?
items.explanation: Pairs are (0,6), (1,5), (2,4); the middle character stays. That is 3 swaps.

items.prompt: You must check whether a string has all distinct characters, scanning it once. Which approach does this in time proportional to the string's length (for a fixed alphabet)?
options: Compare every pair of characters with two nested loops
Sort the string, then compare neighbours
Keep a set of characters seen so far and stop at the first repeat
Split the string in half recursively and compare the halves
items.explanation: A set gives constant-time checks per character, so one pass is enough. Nested loops are quadratic and sorting is n log n.

items.prompt: What is the average time to look up a key in a well-designed hash map?
items.explanation: A good hash function spreads keys across buckets, so a lookup goes straight to its bucket.

items.prompt: Two different keys are mapped to the same bucket. What is this called?
items.explanation: Different keys that land in the same bucket collide; maps handle this with chaining or probing.

items.prompt: Why must two keys that are equal always produce the same hash code?
options: So the map uses less memory
So a lookup goes to the same bucket the key was stored in; otherwise it can miss an entry that exists
So the map never needs resizing
items.explanation: Lookup first finds the bucket from the hash. If equal keys hash differently, the entry sits in a different bucket and is not found.

items.prompt: In SQL, what does an INNER JOIN between two tables return?
options: Only rows that have a match in both tables
All rows of the first table, matched or not
items.explanation: INNER JOIN keeps only the row pairs where the join condition is true.

items.prompt: Table A has ids 1, 2, 3. Table B has a_id values 2, 3, 3, 4. How many rows does A INNER JOIN B ON A.id = B.a_id return?
items.explanation: id 2 matches once and id 3 matches twice: 3 rows. id 1 and a_id 4 have no partner.

items.prompt: Which query finds customers who have never placed an order (tables customers and orders, orders.customer_id refers to customers.id)?
options: SELECT c.* FROM customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
SELECT c.* FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL
SELECT c.* FROM customers c RIGHT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
SELECT c.* FROM customers c CROSS JOIN orders o WHERE o.id IS NULL
items.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer; customers with no order get NULLs on the orders side, which the WHERE clause selects.

items.prompt: Which HTTP status code means the requested resource was not found?
items.explanation: 404 Not Found.

items.prompt: Which of these HTTP methods are idempotent by definition (repeating the same request has the same effect as sending it once)?
items.explanation: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent. POST usually creates something new each time.

items.prompt: A response carries the header Cache-Control: no-store. What does it mean?
options: Caches may keep it but must revalidate every time
Only the browser may cache it, for one hour
No cache may store any part of the response
The response may be cached for ever
items.explanation: no-store forbids storing the response at all. no-cache is the one that allows storing but requires revalidation.

items.prompt: Which command shows changes in your working files that have not been staged yet?
items.explanation: git diff compares the working tree with the index (staged snapshot).

items.prompt: You run git add on a file, then edit that file again, then run git commit. Which version of the file is committed?
options: The version at the time of git add
items.explanation: A commit records what is staged. The later edit stays as an unstaged change.

items.prompt: A bad commit is already pushed to a shared branch. Which is the safe way to undo its effect?
options: git reset --hard to the older commit and force-push
git revert the commit, which adds a new commit that undoes it
Delete the .git folder and clone again
git rebase the shared branch onto itself
items.explanation: revert adds a new commit and keeps shared history intact. Rewriting shared history with reset and force-push breaks other people's copies.

items.prompt: Which SQL expression counts the rows in a table?
items.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows.

items.prompt: Which clause filters groups after GROUP BY has computed their aggregates?
items.explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters the groups.

items.prompt: sales has rows (region, amount): (N,10), (N,20), (S,5), (S,5), (S,50). What does SELECT region FROM sales GROUP BY region HAVING SUM(amount) > 30 return?
items.explanation: N sums to 30, which is not greater than 30. S sums to 60.

items.prompt: What is the mean of 2, 4, 6 and 8?
What is the median of 3, 9, 1, 7 and 100?
items.explanation: Sorted: 1, 3, 7, 9, 100. The middle value is 7.

items.prompt: Which of these changes least when one extreme outlier is added to a data set?
items.explanation: The median depends on the middle position, not on how large the extreme values are.

items.prompt: In a hypothesis test, a p-value below your chosen significance level (for example 0.05) leads you to:
options: Accept the null hypothesis as proven
items.explanation: A small p-value is evidence against the null, so you reject it. It says nothing about the size of the effect.

items.prompt: What is a Type I error?
options: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
items.explanation: Type I is a false positive: rejecting a null that is actually true.

items.prompt: A test gives p = 0.03. Which statement is correct?
options: There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
There is a 97% chance the alternative is true
If the null hypothesis were true, results at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
items.explanation: A p-value is a probability about the data given the null, not a probability that the null is true.

items.prompt: In pandas, what does df.shape return?
options: A tuple of (number of rows, number of columns)
items.explanation: shape is (rows, columns).

items.prompt: What does df.groupby('team')['score'].mean() return?
options: The average score for each team
items.explanation: It splits rows by team and averages score within each group.

items.prompt: pd.merge(a, b, on='key') is called with no how argument. Which rows does the result contain?
options: All keys from a, matched or not
All keys from b, matched or not
Only keys present in both a and b
items.explanation: The default is an inner join.

items.prompt: Which chart type is usually best for showing how a value changes over time?
items.explanation: A line connects ordered points and shows trend.

items.prompt: You want to show the relationship between two numeric variables, such as hours studied and exam score. Which chart fits best?
items.explanation: A scatter plot shows each pair and reveals correlation or clusters.

items.prompt: Why should a bar chart's value axis normally start at zero?
options: It makes the chart load faster
Bars encode value by length, so a truncated axis exaggerates differences
items.explanation: Readers compare bar lengths. Cutting the axis makes small differences look large.

items.prompt: Events A and B are independent. P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A and B)?
items.explanation: For independent events, multiply: 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2.

items.prompt: P(A and B) = 0.12 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A given B)?

A disease affects 1% of people. A test is positive for 90% of people who have it and for 9% of people who do not. A person tests positive. What is the probability they have the disease? (Give a decimal.)
What is the dot product of [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6]?
A is a 2×3 matrix and B is a 3×4 matrix. What is the shape of A × B?
items.explanation: The inner sizes (3 and 3) match and disappear; the outer sizes give 2×4.

items.prompt: What is the determinant of the matrix [[2, 1], [1, 3]]?
items.explanation: For [[a, b], [c, d]] the determinant is ad − bc = 2×3 − 1×1 = 5.

items.prompt: A model has very low error on its training data but much higher error on validation data. This suggests:
items.explanation: Memorising the training data without generalising is overfitting.

items.prompt: What does L2 regularization do?
options: Adds a penalty on large weights, shrinking them
Removes all features with low variance
items.explanation: L2 adds the sum of squared weights to the loss, which discourages large weights.

items.prompt: Which of these help reduce overfitting?
options: Make the model much larger without other changes
Stop training when validation loss stops improving
items.explanation: More data, regularization and early stopping all help. A much larger model usually makes overfitting worse.

items.prompt: A classifier gets 90 of 120 test examples right. What is its accuracy as a decimal?
A model predicted 50 positives: 40 were correct (true positives) and 10 were wrong (false positives). What is its precision as a decimal?
items.explanation: Precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP) = 40 ÷ 50 = 0.8.

items.prompt: Only 1% of transactions are fraud. A model that always predicts 'not fraud' is 99% accurate. What does this show?
options: Accuracy can be misleading on imbalanced data; recall for fraud is 0
items.explanation: The model never finds a single fraud case, so recall is 0, yet accuracy looks high.

items.prompt: How many models are trained in 5-fold cross-validation?
items.explanation: One per fold: each fold takes a turn as the validation set.

items.prompt: In k-fold cross-validation, how many times is each example used for validation?
items.explanation: Each example sits in exactly one fold, so it is validated exactly once and used for training in the other k−1 rounds.

items.prompt: You standardise features (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation) and then cross-validate. Where should the mean and standard deviation be computed?
options: On the whole dataset first, for consistency
Only on the training part of each fold, then applied to its validation part
items.explanation: Computing them on the whole dataset lets information from validation rows leak into training.
